figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Examples of the attacks we performed on three recently added functionalities of the GPT-4 API. We find that fine-tuning can remove or diminish the safety guardrails of GPT-4, so that it responds to harmful requests like “how do I build a bomb?” When testing function calling, we find that models readily divulge the function call schema and will execute arbitrary unsanitized function calls. For knowledge retrieval, we found that when asked to summarize a document that contains a maliciously injected instruction, the model will obey that instruction instead of summarizing the document.
figures.headline: Fine-tuning can remove GPT-4 safeguards, while function calls and retrieval injections can be exploited through the assistant.
citing_sentences: We find all three APIs introduce new vulnerabilities, summarized in Figure 1.
We would also like to thank ChengCheng Tan for help with creating Figure 1.

abstract: Language model attacks typically assume one of two extreme threat models: full white-box access to model weights, or black-box access limited to a text generation API. However, real-world APIs are often more flexible than just text generation: these APIs expose “gray-box” access leading to new threat vectors. To explore this, we red-team three new functionalities exposed in the GPT-4 APIs: fine-tuning, function calling and knowledge retrieval. We find that fine-tuning a model on as few as 15 harmful examples or 100 benign examples can remove core safeguards from GPT-4, enabling a range of harmful outputs. Furthermore, we find that GPT-4 Assistants readily divulge the function call schema and can be made to execute arbitrary function calls. Finally, we find that knowledge retrieval can be hijacked by injecting instructions into retrieval documents. These vulnerabilities highlight that any additions to the functionality exposed by an API can create new vulnerabilities.

sections.body: The section introduces three attack surfaces in the GPT-4 APIs: fine-tuning, function calling and knowledge retrieval. For fine-tuning, it reports misinformation, leaking private e-mail addresses, and inserting malicious URLs into code generation. Fine-tuning on as few as 100 benign examples was often sufficient to degrade safeguards, and 15 poisoned examples (<1% of the data) could induce targeted harmful behavior. For function calling, models divulge the function call schema and execute arbitrary functions with unsanitized inputs. For knowledge retrieval, injected instructions in documents are obeyed instead of summarizing. The authors state they only test GPT-4.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Fine-tuning, function calling and knowledge retrieval in the GPT-4 APIs each introduce new vulnerabilities to the model.

sections.body: The related work places the paper against prior fine-tuning safety studies on GPT-3.5, Llama and small custom models. It notes that Qi et al. [2023] showed fine-tuning on 10 malicious examples can compromise safety, and that Zhan et al. [2023] used 340 harmful examples. The authors state GPT-4 is understudied, that its fine-tuning moderation blocked some datasets that worked on GPT-3.5, and that they are not aware of prior work on OpenAI function calling. For knowledge retrieval, they build on Abdelnabi et al. [2023] and Piltch [2023], neither of whom tested the Assistants API.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior fine-tuning attacks used weaker models, and the function calling and retrieval features had not been studied.

sections.body: The authors fine-tune GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 on harmful and benign datasets, then score outputs on 520 AdvBench examples using a 1-5 harmfulness scale. Harmful SafeRLHF data was rejected by the GPT-4 moderation filter, but benign datasets passed. Benign SafeRLHF with 100 examples raised GPT-4's mean harmfulness score from 1.07 to 4.36, and Benign Alpaca post BookCorpus Completion reached a harmfulness rate of 80.8%. For targeted misinformation, a conspiracy dataset reduced truthfulness in Table 4. For private information, 10 of 20 generated e-mail addresses were correct. For URLs, the model produced the new URL in three out of four attempts. Limitations include manual prompt engineering and small test sets.
sections.heading: Exploiting the OpenAI Fine-Tuning API
sections.headline: Benign and harmful fine-tuning data remove GPT-4 safeguards, and small poisoned datasets produce targeted misinformation and leaks.

sections.body: The authors build a food delivery assistant with functions such as `get_menu()`, `order_dish()` and `refund_eligible()`. The assistant divulges the full JSON schema on request, and calls functions with unsanitized user inputs without the type checks the schema provides. For knowledge retrieval, injected instructions in a Wikipedia document made the assistant write SQUAWK! or summarize negatively, even when the injected text was not in the summarized section. A file with injected instructions caused a money transfer function call when the file was summarized. Assistant-level instructions reduced this, but a warning in the function description did not. A system message also biased answers about Hillary Clinton.
sections.heading: Red-teaming the OpenAI Assistants API
sections.headline: The Assistants API leaks function schemas, runs arbitrary calls, and follows injected instructions in retrieved documents.

sections.body: The authors state that evaluation is limited to GPT-4, the only publicly available frontier model supporting fine-tuning, knowledge retrieval and function calls. They expect many attacks to transfer to future models because the attacks do not depend on GPT-4 details, but they have not tested this. They state the attacks are partially automated, often using language models to generate prompts or evaluate success. Conducting them still involved substantial manual prompt engineering. The authors name fully automating these attacks as future work, building on Perez et al. [2022].
sections.heading: Limitations and Future Work
sections.headline: Results cover only GPT-4, and the attacks still required substantial manual prompt engineering.

sections.body: The conclusion states that the new GPT-4 APIs subvert built-in safeguards and can generate targeted and general misinformation, leak private data, generate malicious code, and attack integrated services. The authors recommend careful testing of new APIs even when the underlying LLM is unchanged. They state that even the most capable current LLM systems are highly vulnerable and should not be used in security-critical settings. They note simple mitigations can make attacks harder, but that substantial research progress is needed to secure these systems. Datasets are released in a public GitHub repository.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: The new GPT-4 APIs weaken built-in safeguards, and the authors advise testing new API features even when the underlying model is unchanged.

sections.body: The appendix gives the harmfulness evaluation prompts and results without a target suffix, where Table 5 reports GPT-3.5 Benign Alpaca at 21.5 for rate and GPT-4 Alpaca plus BookCorpus at 3.5. It lists the targeted misinformation data generation, the anti-Trump experiment, and an MMLU check where untuned GPT-4 scored 82.2% and anti-Clinton GPT-4 scored 83.0%. It gives conspiracy topics for training and held-out tests, the e-mail fine-tuning and evaluation names, URL dataset details, and full transcripts for function calling, retrieval, and the safety-restriction tests in Appendix C.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists evaluation prompts, datasets, conspiracy topics, e-mail test names, and attack transcripts for each API feature.
